subject: Post-demo SLO discovery: multi-hop routing, latency & residency clarifications
messages:
From: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.com>
To: Liam Chen <liam.chen@atlashealth.com>
Cc: Camila Reyes <camila_reyes@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 16 May 2026 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Post-demo SLO discovery: multi-hop routing, latency & residency clarifications

Hi Liam — thanks again for the demo today. Quick recap and a short list of clarifying questions so our engineering team can size a proposal and recommend an architecture. I want to make sure we capture the performance and residency constraints before we run any synthetic tests.

Summary of what we heard (please correct if I’ve misstated):
- Traffic profile: customer-facing chat + on-demand document summarization + near-real-time streaming for clinical notes.
- Desired p95 targets: low-latency for short replies; regional residency for EU customers.
- Peak patterns: weekday US business hours, occasional spikes tied to batch uploads.

Clarifying questions (short answers appreciated):
1) Target SLOs – can you confirm target p50/p95 for short responses (<128 tokens) and for long responses (~512 tokens)? If you have separate SLOs for chat vs. batch summarization, please list them.
2) Regional split – approximate % traffic per region (US / EU / APAC) and whether EU traffic must be processed and persisted only within the EU.
3) Concurrency & streaming – expected concurrent streaming sessions per tenant (rough order: 1–5 / 5–20 / 20+). For streaming use-cases, do you need token-by-token streaming or chunked partials every 200–500ms?
4) Throughput – sustained RPS per region and expected burst QPS. Also let us know typical request token length and response token length distributions.
5) Failover policy – acceptable fallback behavior if a regional pool is saturated (failover to another region, fall back to smaller model, queue requests?)

Attachments: we’ll send a short load test plan and a sample SOW template; can you share any internal SLAs or compliance constraints (e.g., PHI handling, retention windows)?

Next steps: if you can reply with the numbers above, Marcus will draft a capacity/reliability proposal and we can schedule a 60–90 minute perf workshop with your infra team.

Thanks — Hannah
Hannah Schmitt
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
hannah.schmitt@redwood.com


From: Liam Chen <liam.chen@atlashealth.com>
To: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.com>
Cc: Priya Rao <priya.rao@atlashealth.com>, Security Team <security@atlashealth.com>
Date: Sat, 16 May 2026 18:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-demo SLO discovery: multi-hop routing, latency & residency clarifications

Thanks Hannah — great recap. Answers inline below.

1) Target SLOs:
- Short replies (<128 tokens): p50 120–150ms, p95 <= 450ms (US & EU).
- Mid replies (~256 tokens): p95 <= 650ms (US & EU).
- Long replies (~512 tokens / long summaries): p95 <= 1200ms (we understand this is harder).
- APAC is lower priority: p95 <= 800ms for short replies is acceptable for now.

2) Regional split & residency:
- US: 62% traffic (core platform users).
- EU: 28% traffic — EU customers require processing and persistent logs to remain in EU (GDPR / local PHI guidance).
- APAC: 10% (mostly read-heavy, can tolerate higher latency).

3) Concurrency & streaming:
- Concurrent streaming sessions per tenant: typical 2–6, spikes up to 18 for a handful of larger customers.
- For streaming clinical notes we need low-latency partials — token-by-token (or 50–100 token chunking every 100–200ms) is fine. Must avoid per-request long polling.

4) Throughput:
- Sustained: US 60 req/s, EU 30 req/s, APAC 10 req/s.
- Burst: US up to 200 req/s for 3–10 minutes during bulk uploads / night processing.
- Typical request token length: input 40–120 tokens; response 50–400 tokens depending on summarization context.

5) Failover policy:
- If the EU pool is saturated, we cannot send EU-customer data outside the EU. For EU traffic the only acceptable option is degrade to a smaller model hosted within EU or queue for up to 30s. For US traffic we accept cross-region failover to EU as a temporary measure.

Attached: atlas-requested-sow.pdf — contains a short compliance/redline doc. Security team (copied) can add more if needed.

Happy to hop on a perf workshop next week.

— Liam
Head of Platform, Atlas Health
liam.chen@atlashealth.com

From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
To: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.com>, Liam Chen <liam.chen@atlashealth.com>
Cc: Camila Reyes <camila_reyes@redwood.com>, Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 18 May 2026 10:04:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-demo SLO discovery: multi-hop routing, latency & residency clarifications

Hi Hannah / Liam — thanks for the details, Liam. Below are practical, ops-oriented recommendations and plausible performance numbers based on our recent benchmarks with similar workloads. I’ve attached a short capacity worksheet (redwood-region-capacity-proposal.xlsx) with per-route estimates — happy to walk through live.

High-level recommendation:
- For Atlas’ mix (steady sustained load + short bursts + residency constraints) we recommend Dedicated reserved pools in US and EU for customer-facing chat and streaming routes, with a small Hosted fallback tier for non-residency-sensitive workloads in APAC. Dedicated gives predictable p95 under burst and avoids noisy-neighbor issues for PHI workloads.

Numbers & tuning (short responses ~ <128 tokens):
- Baseline observed on our 80GB-A100-like nodes with optimized kernels and 8-bit quantization: p50 ~ 70–120ms, p95 ~ 250–420ms at modest batching. With tighter batching windows and prefix caching we regularly hit p95 <= 350ms for well-cached routes.
- For long responses (~512 tokens) expect p95 700–1400ms depending on batching and sequence length.

Concurrency / capacity planning:
- Concurrency per GPU: design for 6–10 concurrent short-response slots per GPU for low-latency routes; scale concurrency down for streaming-heavy sessions where per-session state (KV cache) uses memory.
- Batching window: recommend adaptive batching with a 8–12ms micro-batch window for chat routes to keep latency tight but still get batching benefits.
- Burst strategy: reserved capacity sized for sustained RPS (US 60/s, EU 30/s) plus 2–3x transient headroom for burst absorption; autoscale delta to cover 10–15s granularity spikes. For the US peak bursts to 200/s plan for a short-term surge capacity (warm pool) rather than cold provisioning — warm pools cost less than cold spin-up for sub-10min surges.

Streaming specifics:
- Token streaming: token-by-token streaming yields the lowest perceived latency but increases per-request RPCs. We recommend chunked streaming (50–100 token partials every 100–200ms) as the middle ground for Atlas — it reduces RPC overhead while keeping UX snappy. If Atlas insists on strict token-at-a-time, we can support it but will reserve additional concurrency slots for streaming sessions.
- Keepalives & idle eviction: set client keepalive at 30s and server-side idle eviction at 45–60s to free streaming slots.

Data residency & failover behavior:
- EU customers: do not route EU traffic outside EU. Fallback behavior: degrade to a smaller quantized family (8-bit QAT or int8) hosted inside EU — typical p95 of that fallback is 600–900ms for short replies, but it preserves residency. Queue behavior: we can queue for up to 30s as requested; beyond that, return 429 with a retry-after header.
- US customers: cross-region failover to EU is acceptable in emergencies but prefer AS/US fallback routes first.

Next steps / deliverables we’ll provide:
1) A short load harness and step-by-step runbook for Atlas to run an initial synthetic test (I’ll upload load_test_plan.xlsx to the shared drive).
2) A Dedicated capacity cost/profile (per-region) and a warm-pool sizing worksheet (attached).
3) Proposed test window: 2 hours of staged ramp tests (sustained + 3x burst) followed by 30m streaming-heavy test to validate streaming concurrency.

If this looks OK, Hannah can schedule a 90-minute perf workshop with our infra team and Atlas’ platform folks. Happy to pair on the test run.

Regards,
Marcus Lin
